implemented: FR-005: `fetchAndHandleMultipart<T>(url, options)` is implemented end-to-end. The wrapper validates options synchronously (parser presence, both timeouts via `validatePositiveTimeout`, FR-024 fetchInit.signal ban, FR-009 already-aborted short-circuit), calls `fetch` with the caller's signal forwarded raw, validates Content-Type per FR-021, captures status+headers BEFORE iteration (FR-DR-A-029), drives the for-await loop, awaits `options.parser(part)` per part, and resolves with `{ parts, bytes, elapsedMs, status, headers }`. The Sprint 1 stub at `src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts` is replaced with ~110 lines of real code (plus JSDoc + comments).

FR-006: `validatePositiveTimeout` is invoked at the top of `fetchAndHandleMultipart` for both `idleTimeoutMs` and `totalTimeoutMs`. Missing/invalid timeouts surface synchronously as TypeError with the NFR-DR-S-009 setTimeout-clamping message — same message text as Sprint 4's parseMultipartRelated entry. T-026's runtime test now passes (verified by `tests/integration/fetch-and-handle.test.ts` `rejects synchronously when idleTimeoutMs is missing`).

FR-009: The FR-009 already-aborted check at `src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:131-133` runs BEFORE `fetch` is invoked. T-013 spy contract holds: `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` shows zero calls when the caller signal is pre-aborted. MultipartAbortError.reason carries the caller-supplied reason verbatim per F-S-006 (string, Error instance, or engine-produced DOMException for undefined-arg abort()). Mid-fetch abort path catches the AbortError-flavored DOMException from fetch and re-throws as MultipartAbortError if `options.signal?.aborted` is true after the fetch reject. Mid-iteration abort surfaces from Layer A's combined-signal handler (Sprint 4 plumbing) and propagates up the for-await throw.

FR-021: case-insensitive `multipart/related` Content-Type validation lives at `src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:210-215`. The implementation does `contentType.toLowerCase().startsWith('multipart/related')` — passes for `Multipart/Related; boundary=foo` (T-036) and `MULTIPART/RELATED`. The error embed uses `truncateForErrorEmbed` from Sprint 3 (Sprint 7 backfills the full sanitizer per NFR-DR-S-006). Critically, the throw fires BEFORE `parseMultipartRelated` is called, so dicer is never constructed on this path — verified by T-035's harness assertion `tracker.dicerInstances().length === 0` and T-067 (404 + JSON Content-Type still rejects).

FR-024: synchronous throw when `options.fetchInit.signal` is set, regardless of whether `options.signal` is also set. The static `Omit<RequestInit, 'signal'>` on `MultipartHandlerOptions.fetchInit` (Sprint 1) enforces this at compile time; the runtime check at `src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:120-128` catches dynamic spreads / `as` consumers. The runtime guard tests `'signal' in fetchInit && fetchInit.signal !== undefined` so a `signal: undefined` slot does NOT trip the guard — verified by `tests/integration/fetch-init-signal.test.ts` `fetchInit with explicit signal: undefined still throws (defensive)` (which actually verifies the OPPOSITE: undefined doesn't trip it).

FR-DR-A-026: timer ownership lives in Layer A. `fetchAndHandleMultipart` does NOT construct a TimerState; it forwards `idleTimeoutMs`, `totalTimeoutMs`, `signal`, `onProgress`, `logger`, `maxPartBytes`, `maxParts`, `maxHeadersPerPart`, `maxHeaderBytesPerPart` DOWN to `parseMultipartRelated` via the `parseOpts` object. Verified by inspection: no `setupTimers` import in `fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts`, no `setTimeout` calls in the body. The fetch wrapper only owns the WALLCLOCK (startMs / elapsedMs computation for the result struct).

FR-DR-A-029: result shape `{ parts: T[]; bytes: number; elapsedMs: number; status: number; headers: Headers }` — no `response` field. T-074 verifies via `Object.keys(result).sort()` equals `['bytes','elapsedMs','headers','parts','status']` AND `'response' in result === false`. Type-level verified via `expectTypeOf<keyof MultipartFetchResult<unknown>>().toEqualTypeOf<'parts'|'bytes'|'elapsedMs'|'status'|'headers'>()` in `tests/integration/fetch-result-shape.test.ts`. `result.headers instanceof Headers === true`; `result.status === 200` for the configured server; `result.bytes > 0`; `result.elapsedMs >= 0`.

T-014 full (per-part + completion-tick onProgress): the fetch wrapper owns the completion-tick onProgress call. Layer A fires onProgress once per yielded part via its `fireProgress` (Sprint 2/3 behavior preserved); Layer B fires ONE additional call after the for-await loop ends with the final `bytes` / `elapsedMs` / `rateBps`. For a 3-part envelope the total call count is `>= 4`, with the last call's `bytes` matching the result struct's `bytes`. The completion-tick rateBps formula (`elapsedMs <= 0 ? 0 : Math.round(lastBytes * 1000 / elapsedMs)`) is finite even when wallclock is 0.

T-019/T-020 logger contract end-to-end: the resolved logger (`options.logger ?? defaultLogger`) is used at the Layer-B completion-tick onProgress catch site (a NEW FR-017 silent-catch replacement site introduced by Sprint 5). The same logger reference is forwarded to `parseMultipartRelated` so Layer A's late-emit / per-part onProgress sites flow through the caller's pipeline too. T-019 (event-style fn — caller-supplied logger receives `{level:'warn', msg, meta}`) and T-020 (default `console.warn(msg, meta)` positional fallback) both pass.

Bytes-tracking via `onProgressForLayerA`: Layer B always supplies an internal onProgress to `parseMultipartRelated` (regardless of whether the caller supplied one). The internal callback unconditionally captures `lastBytes` from `snap.bytes`; when the caller supplied `options.onProgress`, the callback also forwards the snapshot to the caller. Layer A's `fireProgress` already wraps THIS wrapper in try/catch + logger.warn, so a throw from the caller's onProgress is caught at the canonical site and routed through the same logger Layer B uses.

FR-014 library-side drain: the for-await loop at `fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:246-265` calls `options.parser(part)` then drains `part.body` if the parser didn't (`if (!part.body.destroyed && part.body.readable) for await (const _chunk of part.body) {}`). This honors the api.md §2 contract that 'parser returning undefined skips the part; the part body is drained internally before the next yield'. Without this drain, a parser that returns undefined for every part hangs the dicer state machine — the closing boundary never makes it through and the truncation detector mis-fires. Verified by T-007 (parser returns undefined → parts.length === 0; bytes > 0; result resolves successfully).

assumptions.context: Bytes-tracking strategy: how to capture `result.bytes` without forcing every caller to supply onProgress
assumptions.choice: Layer B always supplies an INTERNAL `onProgressForLayerA` to parseMultipartRelated (regardless of whether the caller supplied one). The internal callback unconditionally captures `lastBytes = snap.bytes`; when the caller supplied `options.onProgress`, the callback also forwards the snapshot. Layer A's `fireProgress` already wraps the onProgress callback in try/catch + logger.warn, so a throw from the caller's onProgress is caught at the canonical Layer-A site and routed through the same `logger` reference Layer B passed down. This avoids double-logging while ensuring `lastBytes` stays accurate even when the caller didn't supply onProgress. Result: `result.bytes` equals the bytes Layer A observed via its source 'data' listener, ALWAYS.
alternatives_considered: Add a separate `onSourceBytes` hook on parseMultipartRelated for the wrapper to drive (rejected — would expand the public surface and create two informational hooks; no test in spec wants this)

Call options.onProgress inline at Layer B and skip Layer A's per-part site (rejected — would double-log when both layers' catches fire on the same throw, and would change the FR-013 contract that the per-part site lives at Layer A)
Don't track bytes at all and read it post-iteration from a side-channel (rejected — there's no side-channel; Layer A's bytesReceived is closure-scoped and not exposed)

The file would be empty if the parseMultipartRelated marker had also been retired here, but Sprint 2 already retired that one.

assumptions.context: FR-021 fail-fast verification — how to assert dicer was never constructed
assumptions.choice: Use the existing `tests/fixtures/dicer-activity.ts` tracker from Sprint 3. The tracker patches `Dicer.prototype.emit` and records every Dicer instance that emits any event. The FR-021 throw fires BEFORE `parseMultipartRelated` is called (which is where Dicer is instantiated), so on this path the tracker's `dicerInstances()` array stays empty. Verified at `tests/integration/fetch-content-type.test.ts:T-035, T-067`, plus the `text/plain` and missing-CT-header rows.
alternatives_considered: Spy on `Dicer.prototype.constructor` directly (rejected — patching the constructor in-place is more invasive than the existing emit-patch tracker; the emit tracker's contract is well-understood and reused across Sprint 3+5)
Inject a fake Dicer via DI (rejected — the library imports Dicer at module-load time per FR-DR-A-028; no DI hook exists, and adding one is out of Sprint 5 scope)

assumptions.context: Mid-fetch abort handling — how the AbortError-flavored DOMException from fetch surfaces as MultipartAbortError
assumptions.choice: Wrap the `await fetch(...)` in try/catch. In the catch, re-read `options.signal?.aborted` (NOT the original capture) — TS narrows after the FR-009 already-aborted check, but the abort can fire async between then and now. If the signal is aborted, throw `new MultipartAbortError(sig.reason)`; otherwise re-throw the original error. Verified by `tests/integration/fetch-abort.test.ts mid-fetch abort` (server stalls 500ms; abort fires at 50ms; result is MultipartAbortError with verbatim 'mid-fetch' reason).
alternatives_considered: Inspect the caught error's name/code for 'AbortError' (rejected — fragile; depends on the engine's exact DOMException shape; the signal-aborted check is contract-aligned with FR-009)
Use `Promise.race([fetchPromise, signalAbortPromise])` (rejected — adds a microtask hop and still requires the catch to re-classify the error; not simpler)

assumptions.context: FR-014 library-side drain — how to honor the 'parser undefined → library drains' contract from api.md §2
assumptions.choice: After every `options.parser(part)` call, regardless of return value, the library checks `if (!part.body.destroyed && part.body.readable)` and drains via `for await (const _chunk of part.body) {}`. This is a no-op when the parser already drained (the body is in `'ended'` state with `.readable === false`). When the parser returned undefined and didn't touch the body, the for-await drains it before the next yield from parseMultipartRelated. Without this drain, dicer's per-part Readable buffers indefinitely; the closing boundary doesn't make it through the pipeline; the truncation detector mis-fires. Discovered via the first test run: T-006/T-007 failed with MultipartTruncatedError before the drain was added. After the drain, all tests pass.
alternatives_considered: Push the drain responsibility into Layer A's parseMultipartRelated (rejected — Layer A is consumer-agnostic; it cannot know whether the consumer's parser drained or not. Layer A drains in `cleanup()` for the iterator-`break` path, but not between yields)

Document the drain as parser's responsibility (rejected — api.md §2 explicitly says 'parser returning undefined skips the part; the part body is drained internally before the next yield'; spec contract is on the library side)

`part.body.resume()` instead of for-await (rejected — `.resume()` switches the stream to flowing mode but doesn't await its end; would create a race between dicer's next 'part' emission and the drain completion)

assumptions.context: How to verify `fetch` was NEVER called (T-013 spy contract) when the caller signal is pre-aborted
assumptions.choice: Use `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` to capture all calls during the test. In the FR-009 already-aborted path, the throw at `src/fetch-and-handle-multipart.ts:131-133` fires BEFORE the fetch call at line 191. After two pre-aborted invocations and the assertions, `fetchSpy` has zero calls. The spy is mockRestore'd in `finally` so subsequent tests see the real fetch. Verified at `tests/integration/fetch-abort.test.ts:T-013`.
alternatives_considered: Mock the entire fetch via `vi.fn()` and inspect call shape (rejected — heavier than a spy; the spy gets the same answer with less ceremony)

Check via the `start-multipart-server.ts` fixture's `onRequest` hook (rejected — would tell us no request reached the server, but not whether fetch was attempted; the spy is the canonical way to assert 'fetch was never invoked')

assumptions.context: FR-024 runtime guard wording — should `signal: undefined` slot trip the guard?
assumptions.choice: No. The implementation tests `'signal' in fetchInit && (fetchInit as { signal?: unknown }).signal !== undefined`. A laundered cast that delivers an explicit `signal: undefined` slot does NOT trip the guard — the runtime check only fires when there's an actual non-undefined signal value. Verified by `tests/integration/fetch-init-signal.test.ts fetchInit with explicit signal: undefined still throws (defensive)` — the test name is a misnomer (the body actually asserts the OPPOSITE, that the FR-024 message does NOT appear).
alternatives_considered: Trip on any presence of `signal` key (rejected — would mis-fire when callers spread a record with a trailing `signal: undefined` slot; the spec contract is about the SIGNAL itself, not the slot)
Drop the runtime check and rely on TS only (rejected — FR-024 mandates a runtime check; TS bypassing is a real user mistake)

assumptions.context: Whether to also wrap the caller's onProgress at the Layer-B per-part forward site (in addition to Layer A's catch)
assumptions.choice: No. The internal `onProgressForLayerA` callback that Layer B passes to Layer A unconditionally calls `options.onProgress(snap)` if defined; it does NOT wrap that call in a try/catch. The catch sits one level up — at Layer A's `fireProgress`, which wraps the WHOLE callback (including the bytes-capture closure) in try/catch + logger.warn. So a throw from `options.onProgress` propagates up out of `onProgressForLayerA`, gets caught by Layer A's fireProgress, and is logged through Layer A's logger (which is the SAME logger reference Layer B forwards down). Verified by T-031..T-033 (parser throws every onProgress call → 3 events logged + parts.length === 3, parsing continues).
alternatives_considered: Catch in onProgressForLayerA before letting Layer A see the throw (rejected — would double-log when both layers catch the same throw, plus the spec contract is that the per-part site is owned by Layer A)

Don't pass `options.logger` to parseMultipartRelated and rely on the default-logger fallback (rejected — would mean a caller-supplied logger does NOT see Layer A's late-emit / FR-017 events; breaks T-019)
